llm.summary: The skill's instructions are broadly consistent with a local memory-replacement plugin, but it asks you to install an unvetted npm plugin (and platform binaries), change global OpenClaw configuration, register recurring maintenance jobs, and collect LLM/embedding API keys without declaring them — all of which warrant caution before installation.

dimensions.detail: The name/description (replace built-in memory with layered semantic memory) matches the instructions: installing an OpenClaw plugin, starting local services (Qdrant, cortex-mem-service), and migrating existing memory are all reasonable for a memory system. Minor inconsistency: the docs include Linux config paths while explicitly claiming only macOS Apple Silicon and Windows x64 are supported.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The SKILL.md instructs the agent to modify global OpenClaw settings (enable plugin, disable built-in memory), install an external npm plugin (which will install platform-specific binaries), create and write config files containing LLM/embedding API keys, start/auto-start local services, run maintenance cron jobs every 3 hours, and migrate existing memory by reading files under ~/.openclaw/workspace/memory. These actions go beyond mere 'reading a docs file' and include persistent system changes and access to user data — appropriate for a memory plugin, but high-impact and should be reviewed before execution.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no code in the skill package itself; the runtime instructions direct installation from the npm registry (openclaw plugins install @memclaw/plugin), which will pull platform-specific binary packages as optional dependencies. Using npm is common for this kind of plugin, but it means you will be running external, unreviewed code/binaries not included in the skill bundle; that increases risk and should be audited.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The registry metadata declares no required environment variables, but the instructions require the user to provide LLM and embedding API endpoints and API keys and to store them in plugin settings or config.toml. The SKILL.md also states cortex-mem-service may fall back to environment variables if sections are missing. These secrets are necessary for the plugin’s function, but they are not declared in the skill metadata — an inconsistency that makes it harder to reason about what credentials will be needed or where they will be stored.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The plugin is designed to register automated maintenance (a cron job every 3 hours), auto-start local services, and modify global OpenClaw configuration (disabling built-in memory). While these behaviors are plausible for a memory replacement, they confer persistent presence and the ability to act on user data periodically. Because the skill instructs installing external binaries that implement this behavior, this is a meaningful privilege increase and should be accepted only after review.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill is an instruction-only wrapper that tells the agent to install an external npm plugin and platform binaries, edit your OpenClaw configuration to replace built-in memory, run local services (Qdrant and cortex-mem-service), and store your LLM/embedding API keys in local config files. Recommended precautions before installing: 1) Review the @memclaw/plugin and related npm packages' source code and npm publisher information (the skill package provides no homepage or source link). 2) Backup your OpenClaw config and existing memory files before migration. 3) Limit the scope of any API keys you provide (use separate keys/accounts with minimal privileges and billing limits). 4) Verify the platform/binary packages are from a trusted publisher and inspect what the binaries do (cron job creation, network listeners, and file access). 5) If you cannot inspect the plugin/binaries, treat this as untrusted: do not install on a sensitive machine or with your main API keys. The presence of undisclosed env fallback and the cron job behavior are the main reasons for caution.
